title: AI Therapy Apps: Do They Actually Work?
description: Honest review of AI mental health apps like Woebot, Wysa, and ChatGPT-based therapy. What research shows, limitations, and when to use (or avoid) them.

content.text: AI chatbots promising mental health support are everywhere. But can an algorithm really help with depression and anxiety? Here's what the evidence shows.
Current AI mental health tools fall into three categories:

items: Purpose-built bots (Woebot, Wysa) - designed by psychologists with specific therapeutic frameworks
General AI with mental health features (ChatGPT, Claude) - not designed for therapy but often used for it
Therapist-augmentation tools (AI scribes, session summaries) - support human therapists

content.text: A Stanford RCT found Woebot significantly reduced depression symptoms over 2 weeks, comparable to an information-only control.
content.citation: Fitzpatrick et al., JMIR Mental Health, 2017

content.text: Woebot delivers CBT-based content through a friendly chatbot. It's FDA-cleared for adults and has the most research backing.
Studies show Wysa users report reduced depression and anxiety symptoms, though effect sizes are modest and dropout rates high.

No clinical trials. Anecdotal reports range from 'surprisingly helpful' to 'gave dangerous advice.' These systems aren't designed for mental health and have no safety guardrails for crisis situations.

items: Reduce wait time for some support

content.text: AI chatbots have given harmful advice to suicidal users. Never rely on AI for crisis support. Call 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) or go to your nearest ER.

items: Mild symptoms while waiting for a therapist
When cost is a barrier (apps are usually free or cheap)

content.text: AI therapy apps are tools, not treatments. For mild symptoms, they can teach useful skills and provide some support. But they're not a substitute for human therapy, and they can be actively harmful for people in crisis. Use them as a supplement, not a replacement.
